passages.title: Walking and happiness（開発用）
passages.text:
In 1998, a small group of researchers at a university in northern Europe began a project that, at first, attracted little attention. Their goal was simple: to find out whether people who walk to work are happier than those who drive. "We expected a small difference," said Dr. Anna Lindqvist, who led the study, "but the results surprised everyone." Over five years, the team followed more than 2,000 adults (aged 25 to 60) in three cities. Participants who walked or cycled reported higher levels of satisfaction, and they were less likely to suffer from stress-related illness. Interestingly, the effect did not depend on income; wealthy and poor participants benefited equally.

Why should walking make such a difference? One explanation is physical: exercise releases chemicals in the brain that improve mood. Another is social. People on foot meet their neighbors, notice changes in their town, and feel that they belong to a community. Drivers, by contrast, spend their journeys alone, often in traffic jams that make them angry before the working day has even started. The researchers didn't claim that cars are bad — many participants had no choice but to drive — but they argued that cities should be designed so that walking is a realistic option.

Not everyone agreed with the conclusions. Some critics pointed out that people who choose to walk may already be healthier and happier than those who don't. In other words, walking might be a result of happiness rather than its cause. Lindqvist accepted this criticism, yet she insisted that the overall pattern was too strong to ignore. "If even half of the effect is real," she wrote in 2004, "it is worth building a few more sidewalks."

Today, more than twenty years later, the study is still quoted by city planners around the world. What began as a modest experiment has become part of a larger debate about how we should live, and it reminds us that the simplest habits are sometimes the most important.

passages.title: The Power of Urban Gardening（開発用・ユーザー提供）
passages.text:
Reading Passage: The Power of Urban Gardening

In recent years, urban gardening has gained widespread popularity in major cities around the world. As urban areas expand and concrete structures replace natural landscapes, many city dwellers are looking for ways to reconnect with nature. Urban gardening, which involves growing plants, vegetables, and fruits in small spaces such as rooftops, balconies, and community lots, offers a practical solution to this problem.

One of the primary benefits of urban gardening is its positive impact on the environment. Plants absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen, helping to clean the air in polluted city environments. Furthermore, rooftop gardens can lower building temperatures during hot summer months, reducing the need for air conditioning and conserving energy.

Beyond environmental advantages, urban gardening also promotes social connection and personal health. Community gardens bring neighbors together, fostering a sense of belonging and mutual support among residents. Additionally, growing one's own food encourages a healthier diet rich in fresh produce while providing a relaxing activity that reduces stress. Although limited space and soil quality can present challenges, innovative methods like vertical farming are making urban agriculture more accessible than ever.

passages.title: Rethinking Our Relationship with Technology（開発用・ユーザー提供）
passages.text:
Reading Passage: Rethinking Our Relationship with Technology

In today's hyper-connected world, smartphones and constant internet access have made our lives far more convenient. However, this non-stop digital interaction comes with a price. Many people experience increased anxiety, reduced attention spans, and a feeling of being constantly overwhelmed. In response to these challenges, the concept of a "digital detox" — intentionally taking a break from electronic devices — has gathered significant attention.

A digital detox does not mean abandoning technology altogether. Instead, it encourages individuals to establish healthy boundaries. For example, some people choose to turn off notifications during dinner, while others set aside entire weekends to stay offline. Research shows that taking brief breaks from screens can improve sleep quality, enhance face-to-face communication, and boost overall mental well-being.

Despite these benefits, practicing a digital detox can be difficult due to work obligations and social expectations. To make it manageable, experts suggest starting small, such as creating phone-free zones at home or replacing late-night screen time with reading a physical book. By making conscious choices about when and how we use technology, we can regain control over our time and mental energy.
